unit.title: Comply with infection prevention and control policies and procedures

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is a 'pathogen'?
options: A chemical that kills germs on tools
A skin rash that is caused by a product
A germ that can make a person ill
A machine that sterilises metal tools

questions.stem: A comb used on one client is used on the next client without being cleaned. Germs pass from the first client to the second. What is this way of spreading called?
options: Indirect contact
Airborne spread
Direct contact
Spread by food

questions.stem: Which of these is a 'way in' (portal of entry) for germs into the body?
options: Clean, unbroken skin on the upper arm
Hair that has been freshly washed
Nails that are filed short and smooth
A small cut or graze on the hand

questions.stem: Infection control is often explained as a 'chain of infection'. What is the aim of good practice?
options: To find out which client first brought the germ into the salon
To break the chain at one or more of its links
To make the germs weaker before they spread
To let clients build up their own immunity

questions.stem: Which client is most likely to pick up an infection easily?
options: A healthy young adult with no cuts
A client whose immune system is weak
A client who washed her hands on arrival
A client who has had all her vaccines

questions.stem: What are 'standard precautions'?
options: Extra steps used only for clients who say they are ill
Rules that apply only to the staff who give massages
The cleaning done once a week when the salon is closed for the day
Safe steps used with every client, every time, to stop germs

questions.stem: Where should a therapist find the steps for infection control in the salon where she works?
options: The Centre's infection control policy and procedures
A friend who has worked in another salon for many years
Any video she finds on social media
The client's own advice on cleaning

questions.stem: Who is responsible for following the infection control procedures in a salon?
options: Only the manager, who writes the salon policy
Only the cleaner, who cleans the salon at night
Every member of staff and every trainee
Only the staff who use sharp tools or wax

questions.stem: A salon's infection control policy should be based on which of these?
options: What the busiest therapist likes to do
The cheapest products the salon can buy
Whatever the last owner of the salon did
Ministry of Health and Wellness guidance

questions.stem: When must a therapist clean her hands?
options: Before and after touching each client
Only when the hands look dirty
Only once, at the start of each day
Only after using the staff toilet

questions.stem: When you wash your hands, how long should you rub them together with soap before rinsing?
options: A quick rinse of about 5 seconds
Only as long as it takes to wet them
At least 20 seconds
About 10 seconds

questions.stem: When should you wash with soap and water instead of using an alcohol hand rub?
options: When you are about to greet a new client at the desk
When your hands are visibly dirty or soiled
When you have just put on a fresh apron
When you have only touched the till

questions.stem: An alcohol hand rub works well against most germs if it contains at least how much alcohol?
After washing your hands, how should you dry them?
options: On the front of your uniform
On the towel the last client used for her feet
By shaking them in the air
With a clean, single-use paper towel

questions.stem: Why should a therapist keep her nails short and take off rings before treatments?
options: Because rings make massage strokes much slower
So that clients can see their own nails clearly
Because germs collect under long nails and rings
So that gloves last longer and cost less

questions.stem: When should a therapist change her disposable gloves?
options: At the end of the working day
Between every client, and if they tear
Only when they start to feel sticky
After every third client

questions.stem: A therapist wears gloves for a wax treatment. Which is correct when she takes them off?
options: Clean her hands straight after taking them off
Wash the gloves and use them on the next client
Put them in her pocket to use later
Leave them on the trolley for the cleaner

questions.stem: Why might a therapist wear a disposable apron over her uniform?
options: To make the uniform look more modern
To keep the uniform warm in the treatment room
To protect the uniform from splashes and germs
So that clients know who the senior therapist is

questions.stem: When should a therapist wear eye protection, such as goggles?
options: When greeting clients at the reception desk
When booking client appointments by phone
When folding clean towels in the store room
When mixing or pouring disinfectant

questions.stem: When you take off your PPE after a treatment, which item usually comes off first?
options: Your mask
Your gloves
Your visor
Your apron

questions.stem: What does 'cleaning' a tool mean?
options: Killing every germ on it, including spores, with steam under pressure
Soaking the tool in disinfectant for one minute
Removing dirt, hair and product with detergent and water
Wiping the tool on a towel between clients

questions.stem: What does 'disinfection' do?
options: Kills most germs on surfaces and tools
Removes dirt but kills no germs
Kills every germ, including spores
Makes metal tools shiny and smell fresh again

questions.stem: What does 'sterilisation' do?
options: Removes loose hair from tools
Kills all germs, including spores
Kills only the germs you can see
Hides germs under a protective film

questions.stem: Why must a tool be cleaned before it is disinfected?
options: Because disinfectant does not work on metal
So the disinfectant smells less strongly
Because cleaning alone makes the tool fully sterile
Dirt and product stop disinfectant reaching germs

questions.stem: The label on a disinfectant gives a 'contact time'. What is this?
options: How long the opened bottle can be kept
How long you must wait after use before touching a client
How long the surface or tool must stay wet with it
How long you must wear gloves after using it

questions.stem: How should a disinfectant solution for soaking tools be prepared?
options: Diluted exactly as the maker's instructions say
Made stronger than the label says, to be safe
Mixed with another cleaner to work faster
Diluted by guessing, if it smells strong

questions.stem: Which piece of equipment uses steam under pressure to sterilise metal tools?
options: A UV cabinet
A towel warmer
A wax heater
An autoclave

questions.stem: In most salons, what is an ultraviolet (UV) cabinet used for?
options: Sterilising tools straight after use, without cleaning them
Storing tools that have already been disinfected
Drying wet towels between clients
Warming wax and paraffin before use

questions.stem: After metal tweezers have been cleaned and disinfected, where should they be kept?
options: Loose in the therapist's apron pocket
On the trolley with the used tools
In a clean, closed and labelled container
In the disinfectant jar until the next day, or longer

questions.topic: Single-use items and the work area
questions.stem: What should be done with a wooden orange stick after it has been used on one client?
options: Throw it away after that client
Rinse it under the tap and reuse it
Soak it in disinfectant and reuse it
Keep it for the same client

questions.topic: Single-use items and the work area
questions.stem: During a wax treatment, why must the therapist never put a used spatula back into the wax pot ('double dipping')?
options: It cools the wax down too much
It can put the client's germs into the wax
It makes the wax too thick to spread
It wastes wax that the salon has already paid for

questions.topic: Single-use items and the work area
questions.stem: How should the couch roll (paper sheet) on a treatment couch be handled?
options: Changed once a day, in the morning before opening
Changed only when it looks dirty
Turned over for the next client
Replaced with fresh roll for each client

questions.stem: Where must a used single-use blade be put?
options: In the general waste bin
Wrapped in tissue in the bin
In a rigid sharps box
In the paper recycling bin

questions.stem: When should a sharps box be closed and sent for collection?
options: When it is filled to the fill line
Only when it is full to the very top
When it starts to rattle
At the end of every year

questions.stem: A therapist cuts her finger on a used blade. What should she do first?
options: Suck the wound to clean it out
Let it bleed and wash it with soap and water
Scrub it hard with a nail brush and some bleach
Cover it with a plaster and carry on working

questions.stem: Before cleaning up a small spill of blood, what should the therapist put on?
options: Nothing, as long as she washes her hands after
A clean apron only
A face mask only
Disposable gloves and an apron

questions.stem: A glass bottle of toner falls and breaks on the floor. How should it be cleared up?
options: Pick up the pieces with bare hands, carefully
Leave it where it is for the cleaner at the end of the day
Wear gloves and sweep it up with a dustpan and brush
Push the pieces under the trolley out of the way

questions.stem: Which waste should go into the clinical (contaminated) waste bag, as the Centre's policy says?
options: Empty product boxes and old paper
Cotton wool soaked with blood
Used razor blades and used needles
Food wrappers from the staff room

questions.stem: How should used towels be handled after a client?
options: Put in a covered laundry bin, then washed hot
Folded and put back on the shelf if they look clean
Shaken out and used again for the next client
Left on the couch until the end of the day

questions.stem: Which of these infections is spread mainly through contact with infected blood?
options: Athlete's foot
Head lice
Impetigo
Hepatitis B

questions.stem: Which blood-borne infection can staff be protected against with a vaccine?
options: HIV
Hepatitis C
Hepatitis B
Ringworm

questions.stem: A client has crusty, honey-coloured sores around her nose and mouth. This may be impetigo. What should the therapist do?
options: Give the treatment, but wear gloves the whole time
Not treat her, and suggest she sees a doctor
Cover the sores with make-up and carry on
Pop the sores with a sterile lance first

questions.stem: A client has a verruca (a wart) on the sole of her foot and asks for a pedicure. What is the safest choice?
options: Do not treat the foot, and suggest she sees her doctor
File the verruca down with a foot file
Give the pedicure and keep the same file for the next client
Soak the foot longer to soften the verruca

questions.stem: Which of these is a sign of a fungal infection of the nail?
options: A shiny, pink and smooth nail
A white half-moon at the nail base
Small white spots from a knock
A thick, yellow or crumbly nail

questions.stem: Why should a therapist cover a cut on her hand with a waterproof plaster before work?
options: To stop the cut from itching during the working day
So that clients do not ask her about it
To stop germs getting in or blood getting out
So that the cut heals without leaving a mark

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What word describes an item, such as an emery board, that is used on one client only and then thrown away?

A therapist cuts herself on a used blade. On which form must this be written down?
Which government ministry in Jamaica gives guidance on infection prevention and control?
accepted: the Ministry of Health and Wellness

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name for a reason, such as an infection, why a treatment must not be given?

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how a therapist should wash her hands with soap and water in the salon, and say when she should do it.
essays.modelAnswer: Before washing, she takes off rings and her watch and checks that her nails are short and clean. She wets her hands under clean running water and puts on liquid soap from a dispenser. She rubs the palms together, then the back of each hand, between the fingers, around each thumb, the fingertips and nails, and the wrists. She keeps rubbing for at least 20 seconds. She rinses well under running water. She dries her hands fully with a clean paper towel and uses the towel to turn off the tap, unless it is a sensor or elbow tap, then puts the towel in a pedal bin. She washes her hands before and after every client, after taking off gloves, after touching used tools, towels or waste, after using the toilet, and before eating. When her hands look dirty she uses soap and water, not hand rub.
markingPoints: Removes jewellery, wets the hands and uses liquid soap
Rubs every part: palms, backs, between the fingers, thumbs, fingertips and wrists
Rubs for at least 20 seconds, then rinses under running water
Dries fully with a clean paper towel and does not touch the tap with clean hands
Says when: before and after each client, after removing gloves or touching waste, after the toilet, before eating

essays.stem: Explain what personal protective equipment a therapist should use when she cleans a pedicure foot bowl with disinfectant, and how she should take it off safely afterwards.
essays.modelAnswer: Before she starts, she reads the disinfectant label and its safety data sheet, and she opens a window or turns on the extractor fan. She puts on a disposable apron to protect her uniform and skin from splashes, and eye protection, such as goggles, in case the solution splashes into her eyes. She puts on gloves that protect against the chemical, such as nitrile gloves, last, so that they cover her cuffs. If the label says a mask is needed, she wears one. When she has finished, she takes off the gloves first, because they are the most contaminated, peeling them off inside out without touching the outside with bare skin. She then removes the apron by rolling it inwards, and then the eye protection, holding it by the strap. Disposable items go in the correct bin, reusable goggles are cleaned, and she washes her hands straight away.
markingPoints: Reads the label or safety data sheet first and ventilates the room
Apron to protect skin and uniform from splashes
Eye protection against splashes, and gloves such as nitrile put on last
Takes the gloves off first, inside out, without touching the outside
Removes the apron and eye protection, disposes of them correctly and washes her hands

essays.stem: Explain the difference between cleaning, disinfection and sterilisation, and give a salon example of each.
essays.modelAnswer: Cleaning is always the first step. It uses detergent, warm water and a brush to remove dirt, hair, skin, oil and product. It removes many germs but does not kill them all. For example, a therapist scrubs used tweezers in warm soapy water. Disinfection uses a chemical disinfectant, made up as the maker says, to kill most germs on cleaned tools and surfaces, but it may not kill spores. The item must stay wet for the full contact time on the label. For example, the couch and trolley are wiped with disinfectant between clients, and cleaned metal tools are soaked. Sterilisation kills all germs, including spores. It is usually done in an autoclave, which uses steam under pressure. For example, metal tools that may have touched blood, such as cuticle nippers, can be sterilised in an autoclave if the salon has one. An item must be cleaned before it is disinfected or sterilised, or the dirt will protect the germs.
markingPoints: Cleaning removes dirt and product with detergent and water, with an example
Disinfection kills most germs but not always spores, with an example
Sterilisation kills all germs including spores, for example in an autoclave
Items must be cleaned before they are disinfected or sterilised
Follows the maker's instructions, including the contact time

essays.stem: Describe how to clean and disinfect metal tools, such as cuticle nippers and tweezers, between clients.
essays.modelAnswer: I wear gloves, and eye protection when I handle the disinfectant. Straight after the treatment I put the used tools in a tray marked 'used', away from clean tools. I scrub each tool with a brush in warm water and detergent, opening hinged tools such as nippers so the joint is cleaned. I rinse them and check that no hair, skin or product is left, then dry them. I make up fresh disinfectant, diluted exactly as the maker's instructions say, in a container with a lid. I put the tools in so they are fully covered and leave them for the full contact time on the label. I lift them out with clean tongs or clean gloves, rinse them if the maker says to, and dry them with a clean paper towel. I store them in a clean, closed, labelled container until they are needed. I throw away any single-use items and fill in the cleaning log if the salon keeps one.
markingPoints: Keeps used tools apart from clean ones and wears gloves
Scrubs the tools with detergent and water, opening hinges, then rinses and dries them
Soaks them fully in fresh disinfectant made up as the maker says, for the full contact time
Removes them with clean tongs or gloves, and rinses and dries them as directed
Stores them in a clean, closed, labelled container and records the cleaning

essays.stem: Explain how sharps, such as single-use blades, should be handled and disposed of safely in a salon or spa.
essays.modelAnswer: Sharps are items that can cut or pierce the skin, such as single-use blades. Each blade is used on one client only. The therapist handles it with care, never passes it by hand to someone else, and never leaves it lying on the trolley or wrapped in a towel. She does not bend, break or try to put the cover back on a used blade. Straight after use she puts it into a sharps box, which is a rigid, puncture-proof, labelled container. The sharps box is kept upright, close to where sharps are used and out of reach of children and clients, with the lid partly closed between uses. It is filled only up to the fill line, then locked shut and sent for collection by the licensed service, as the Centre's policy says. A sharps box is never emptied out or put in the general waste. Any sharps injury is reported at once.
markingPoints: Single use only; handles sharps with care and never leaves them loose
Does not bend, break or re-cover used sharps
Puts them straight into a rigid, labelled sharps box kept near the work area
Fills the box only to the line, then locks it and sends it for licensed collection; never empties it
Reports any sharps injury at once

essays.stem: Describe how to deal safely with a small spill of blood on the floor of a treatment room.
essays.modelAnswer: First I make sure the client is cared for and keep other people away from the spill. I collect the salon's spill kit. I put on disposable gloves and an apron, and eye protection if there could be splashes. I cover the spill with paper towels, or the absorbent granules in the kit, to soak it up. I lift the soiled towels or granules with the scoop and put them straight into the clinical waste bag. I clean the area with detergent and water, then disinfect it with the product the Centre's policy names, made up as the maker says, and leave it for the contact time. I keep the room ventilated and mark the wet floor. I put all used cloths, my gloves and my apron in the clinical waste bag and seal it. I wash my hands. Then I record the spill and report it to the supervisor, following the Ministry of Health and Wellness guidance and the Centre's policy.
markingPoints: Keeps people away and uses the spill kit
Wears gloves and an apron (and eye protection if needed)
Absorbs the blood and puts the waste into the clinical waste bag
Cleans, then disinfects as the maker says, for the contact time
Disposes of PPE, washes hands, and records and reports the spill

essays.stem: Explain how the different types of salon waste should be sorted and disposed of.
essays.modelAnswer: Waste is sorted where it is made, so that dangerous waste does not end up in the wrong place. General waste, such as paper, packaging and couch roll with no blood on it, goes into a lined bin with a lid, emptied every day. Clinical waste, such as cotton wool, wax strips, gloves or tissues soiled with blood or body fluids, goes into the clinical waste bag the Centre uses. The bag is sealed before it is too full, about three-quarters full or as the policy says, and collected by the licensed service. Sharps, such as used blades, go only into the sharps box. Chemical waste, such as old disinfectant or out-of-date products, is disposed of as the label or safety data sheet says, and chemicals are never mixed together. Clean empty bottles and cardboard can be recycled. Pedal bins mean staff do not touch the lids. Staff wear gloves to handle waste and wash their hands afterwards.
markingPoints: General waste in a lined bin with a lid
Blood-soiled waste in the clinical waste bag, sealed and collected by a licensed service
Sharps only in the sharps box
Chemicals disposed of as the label or safety data sheet says, and never mixed
Uses gloves and pedal bins, and washes hands after handling waste

essays.stem: A client arrives for a manicure and you notice redness, swelling and pus around one of her fingernails. Explain what you should do and why.
essays.modelAnswer: Redness, swelling and pus around a nail can be signs of an infection. An infection is a contraindication, so I should not give the manicure. Working on the hand could spread the infection to her other nails, to me and, through tools and towels, to other clients, and it could make the infection worse. I would explain this to the client calmly and in private. I would not try to tell her what the condition is, because I cannot diagnose; instead I would suggest that she sees her doctor. I would offer to rebook her for when it has cleared up. I would not touch the area. I would write on her record card that the treatment was not given and why. Afterwards I would clean and disinfect the work surface and anything she touched, throw away any single-use items, and wash my hands.
markingPoints: Sees a possible infection, which is a contraindication, so gives no treatment
Explains the risk of spreading the infection and making it worse
Tells the client tactfully and privately, without diagnosing, and refers her to a doctor
Offers to rebook and records it on the record card
Cleans and disinfects the area and washes hands

essays.stem: Explain how blood-borne infections such as hepatitis B and HIV could be spread in a salon, and how staff prevent this.
essays.modelAnswer: Blood-borne infections are carried in blood and some body fluids. In a salon they could spread if blood from an infected person gets into another person's body through a cut, broken skin, the eyes or the mouth. This could happen through a used blade, cuticle nippers that cut the skin, wax that has been double dipped, or a towel with blood on it. A person can carry hepatitis B or HIV and look completely well, so staff treat every client as if they could be infectious. To prevent spread, staff cover their own cuts with waterproof plasters, wear gloves when there is a risk of blood, use single-use items once only, never double dip, clean and then disinfect or sterilise tools, put sharps straight into a sharps box, and deal with blood spills using the spill kit. Staff should also ask their doctor about the hepatitis B vaccine. Any injury or splash is reported at once.
markingPoints: Explains spread through blood entering a cut, broken skin, the eyes or the mouth
Gives salon examples: blades, nippers, double-dipped wax, soiled towels
Treats every client as possibly infectious (standard precautions)
Prevention: gloves, covered cuts, single-use items, decontamination and the sharps box
Hepatitis B vaccine, and reporting injuries at once

essays.stem: Why must staff follow the Centre's infection prevention and control policy, and what kinds of things should be reported and recorded?
essays.modelAnswer: The policy sets out the safe steps everyone must take. It follows the Ministry of Health and Wellness guidance and the Centre's own rules. If every person follows the same steps every time, germs are not passed between clients and staff, clients can trust the salon, and the business protects its good name. If one person cuts corners, everyone is put at risk. Staff should report and record any cut, sharps injury or splash of blood or body fluid; any blood spill and how it was cleaned; signs of infection seen on a client and any treatment that was refused; their own illness, such as fever, diarrhoea or a skin infection; and problems such as a broken autoclave, an empty soap dispenser, a full sharps box or a shortage of PPE. Cleaning and sterilising logs are filled in each day. Reports go to the supervisor in writing, so that problems are put right and patterns can be seen.
markingPoints: The policy follows Ministry of Health and Wellness guidance and keeps clients and staff safe
Everyone follows the same steps every time; one lapse puts everyone at risk
Reports and records injuries, splashes and spills
Reports infections seen, own illness, and faulty or missing equipment
Keeps cleaning logs and incident records and tells the supervisor

practical1.title: Clean, disinfect and reset a manicure and pedicure station between clients
practical1.brief: The assessor sets up a manicure and pedicure station as if a client has just left: used metal tools, a used nail file and orange stick, used towels, cotton wool, a foot bowl with water, and product left on the work surface (a little hand lotion stands for the dirt; no real body fluids are used). As a group, make the station safe for the next client. Before you start, every member washes their hands while the others check the steps, and the group puts on PPE. Share the jobs so that each member leads at least one stage while the others help and check: (1) sort the used items into single-use waste, laundry and tools to be cleaned, (2) scrub the metal tools with a brush, detergent and water, (3) make up the disinfectant as the label says and soak the tools for the full contact time, timed with a clock, (4) clean and then disinfect the work surface, the chair arms and the foot bowl, (5) lift out, dry and store the tools in a clean, closed, labelled container, set out fresh towels and new single-use items, take off PPE safely and fill in the cleaning log. In a group of 4, one member leads two stages. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the station is ready and the cleaning log is signed.
materials: A manicure table and a pedicure chair or foot bowl, set up as used by the assessor
Metal tools: cuticle nippers, cuticle pusher, tweezers and nail clippers
Used single-use items: nail files, orange sticks, cotton wool and couch roll
Detergent, a nail brush and a tray marked 'used'
A salon disinfectant with its label and safety data sheet, a measuring jug and a soaking container with a lid
Disposable gloves, aprons and eye protection
Paper towels, fresh towels, a laundry bin and a pedal bin with a lid
A clean, closed container with a label, and the station cleaning log
A clock or timer, and a phone or camera for photos
photos: Each member washing their hands at the basin (hands only)
The used station before the group starts
The used items sorted into waste, laundry and tools to clean
Tools being scrubbed in detergent and water
The disinfectant measured as the label says, the tools fully covered, and the timer showing
The work surface and foot bowl being disinfected
The clean tools in the closed, labelled container, and the station reset with fresh towels
The completed and signed cleaning log
checklist: Washed hands correctly, covering every part, for at least 20 seconds
Put on PPE in the right order and took it off safely, gloves first, then washed hands
Sorted single-use items, laundry and tools correctly
Cleaned the tools fully before disinfecting them, opening hinged tools
Made up the disinfectant as the label says and kept to the contact time
Cleaned and disinfected all surfaces and the foot bowl
Stored the clean tools in a closed, labelled container away from used items
Reset the station with fresh towels and new single-use items, and filled in the log
safety: Read the disinfectant label and safety data sheet before use, and never mix chemicals
Wear gloves, an apron and eye protection when handling disinfectant, and keep the room ventilated
If disinfectant gets in the eyes, rinse with plenty of clean running water and get help
Wipe up water on the floor straight away so that no one slips
Do not touch the tips of the metal tools with bare hands; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Deal with a blood spill, set up a sharps box and sort salon waste
practical2.brief: The assessor sets two tasks. Task A is a 'blood' spill on the floor of a treatment room, made with red food colouring and water or a training gel (no real blood is used). Task B is a tray of mixed mock salon waste: packaging, clean couch roll, cotton wool stained with the mock blood, used wax strips, empty bottles, an out-of-date product, and a blunt training blade or a new blade still in its cover. As a group, plan who does what, then: (1) set up a new sharps box: put it together, label it with the date and the work area, and place it where the Centre's policy says, (2) deal with the spill: one member keeps other people away while two members put on PPE, soak up, lift and bag the waste, clean, and then disinfect the area as the maker says, (3) sort every item from Task B into general waste, clinical waste, the sharps box, chemical waste or recycling, saying why for each, (4) take off PPE, wash hands, and fill in the spill record and a short report for the supervisor. Every member takes part in the spill clean-up or the sorting, and explains at least two of the group's choices to the assessor. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: A spill kit: gloves, apron, eye protection, absorbent granules or paper towels, a scoop and a clinical waste bag
Mock blood (red food colouring and water, or a training gel)
A new sharps box and a label
A tray of mixed mock waste, including a blunt training blade or a new blade in its cover
A general waste bin, a clinical waste bag and a recycling box
Detergent and the disinfectant named in the Centre's policy, with its label
A spill record sheet and a report form
A wet-floor sign, and a phone or camera for photos
photos: The new sharps box put together, labelled and in place
The spill area kept clear, with the members who clean it in PPE
The spill soaked up and the waste going into the clinical waste bag
The area being cleaned and then disinfected, with the wet-floor sign out
The mixed waste sorted into the correct bins and bags
The sealed clinical waste bag and the closed sharps box
The completed spill record and report
checklist: Put together, labelled and placed the sharps box correctly
Kept others away from the spill and used the spill kit
Wore the right PPE and took it off safely
